deep.reconstruction:
This page is part of Gauss's mathematical diary (Tagebuch, published by Klein 1903, Werke X.1). It covers entries of 3 Aug to 6 Sept 1796, roughly entries 22-31 in the standard numbering. There are no full derivations, only dated statements of results. Each is restated below.

(1) 3 Aug, Göttingen: 'a^{2^n+1} ≡ 1 (mod p) semper solvere in potestate [est]', i.e. 'I can always solve the congruence a^{2^n+1} ≡ 1 (mod p)'. The exact intended problem is unclear, and the reading of the exponent is also uncertain. A plausible context is solving binomial congruences, perhaps by successive square roots in connection with p = 2^n+1 and the 17-gon. No computation is given.

(2) 13 Aug: Gauss has seen how the 'reason' of the theorema aureum (quadratic reciprocity) must be probed more deeply. To that end he tries to go beyond quadratic equations. He records the 'invention of formulas which are always divisible (numerically) by primes [via] the n-th roots of unity'. This is plausibly the idea of treating x^n - 1, or the period polynomials, modulo primes, so that roots of unity exist 'numerically', i.e. modulo p. This is the programme that leads to entry (8).

(3) 14 Aug: 'In passing, (a+b√-1)^{m+n√-1} expanded.' Modern form, with r = sqrt(a^2+b^2) and θ = arg(a+bi) (principal branch):
(a+bi)^{m+ni} = exp((m+ni)(log r + iθ)) = r^m e^{-nθ} [cos(mθ + n log r) + i sin(mθ + n log r)].

(4) 16 Aug: 'The essence of the matter is now understood; it remains to secure the details.' There is no mathematics in this entry.

(5) 18 Aug: '(a^p) ≡ (a) mod p, a root of any equation however irrational.' Here (·) denotes the aggregate, i.e. the sum over all roots of the (monic, integer-coefficient) equation.
- The claim is Σ α_i^p ≡ Σ α_i (mod p).
- Proof (mine): in Z[α_1,...,α_k], (Σα_i)^p ≡ Σα_i^p mod p, since the multinomial coefficients are divisible by p.
- Σα_i = s is an integer, and s^p ≡ s by Fermat's little theorem.
- Σα_i^p is a symmetric integer polynomial in the roots, hence an integer, so the congruence descends to Z.
- This is the trace form of the Frobenius congruence.

(6) 19 Aug: 'If P, Q are algebraic functions [polynomials] of an indeterminate that are incommensurable [coprime], there exist t, u with tP + uQ = 1. This holds in letter-algebra as well as numerically (for integers).' This is the Bézout identity, obtained by the extended Euclidean algorithm in Q[x] and in Z.

(7) 21 Aug: 'The power sums of the roots of a given equation are expressed by the coefficients by a very simple law.' For x^k + c_1 x^{k-1} + ... + c_k with power sums s_m:
s_m + c_1 s_{m-1} + ... + c_{m-1} s_1 + m c_m = 0 for m ≤ k, and
s_m + c_1 s_{m-1} + ... + c_k s_{m-k} = 0 for m > k.
These are Newton's identities. The parenthesis mentions 'other geometers in the Exerc.', which is apparently a reference to a book of Exercitationes.

(8) Same day: summation of 1 + x^n/n! + x^{2n}/(2n)! + ...
With ω = e^{2πi/n}, this equals (1/n) Σ_{j=0}^{n-1} exp(ω^j x), by series multisection using roots of unity. Examples: n=2 gives cosh x; n=3 gives (e^x + 2e^{-x/2} cos(√3 x/2))/3.

(9) 2 Sept, starred: 'Apart from certain minutiae I have happily reached the goal.' Namely, if p^n ≡ 1 (mod π) (π prime), then x^π - 1 is, modulo p, composed of factors of degree not exceeding n. Hence the 'conditional equation' (the congruence) is solvable. 'From which I deduced two new proofs of the golden theorem.'
- In modern terms, with f = ord_π(p): mod p, x^π - 1 = (x-1) · (product of (π-1)/f irreducible factors, each of degree f).
- f divides n, so every factor has degree ≤ n.
- Equivalently, the π-th roots of unity lie in GF(p^f) ⊆ GF(p^n).
- Gauss used this to give proofs of quadratic reciprocity. Compare the posthumously published section VIII of the Disquisitiones and the cyclotomic/Gauss-sum approach.

(10) 6 Sept: 'The number of unequal fractions whose denominators do not exceed a certain limit, compared with the number of all fractions whose numerator or denominator are distinct below the same limit, is in the limit as 6 : π².'
The statement is that #{(a,b) ≤ N : gcd(a,b) = 1} / N^2 → 6/π². Equivalently, Σ_{k≤N} φ(k) ~ 3N^2/π². This is the probability that two random integers are coprime. It builds on the previous page's 20 June entry, where Gauss related Σ 1/n^2 = π²/6 to factor sums.
errors: No outright mathematical errors are visible; the page states results without proofs.
Entry 18 Aug: the congruence requires the equation to be monic with integer coefficients (roots algebraic integers) so that the power sums are integers; this hypothesis is implicit.

Entry 2 Sept: 'factors of degree not exceeding n' is correct but weaker than the truth. All nonlinear factors have the same degree f = ord_π(p), which divides n. Gauss himself notes 'minutiae' still to be settled.
Entry 14 Aug: the expansion of a complex power is multivalued (θ + 2kπ); a single-valued formula presupposes a branch choice.
Entry 3 Aug: as written, the statement is too terse to check; the intended congruence and quantifiers are unclear.

deep.surprise_reason: These are well-known, published entries (about nos. 22–31) of Gauss's mathematical diary, extensively commented on by Klein, Bachmann and Gray. They include the Frobenius-type congruence, cyclotomic factorization mod p and 6/π², all already attributed to Gauss through the diary. Nothing here is new to historians.
